{{Short description|German physicist}}
'''Dieter Langbein''', [[Dr. phil. nat.]], was a German physicist, whose fields of research included [[Solid-state physics|solid state physics]], [[Fluid mechanics|fluid physics]] and [[Micro-g environment|microgravity]]. He was born on 10 February 1932 in [[Frankfurt|Frankfurt am Main]], Germany as Werner Dietrich Langbein and died on 25 June 2004 in [[Bad Homburg vor der Höhe|Bad Homburg]], Germany. He was married and had a son and two daughters.

== Early days ==
In 1951 Dieter Langbein started his studies in [[mathematics]] at the [[Goethe University Frankfurt|Johann Wolfgang Goethe-Universität]] at Frankfurt am Main, where he met Prof. [[Friedrich Hund]] who inspired him to work in [[theoretical physics]]. After his diploma in physics in 1956 and his thesis on solid state physics in 1958 he went to the [[University of Göttingen|Institute of Theoretical Physics]] at [[Göttingen]] to work with Prof. Hund in investigating galvanomagnetic effects.

== Research ==
In 1962 he joined [[Hoechst AG|Farbwerke Hoechst AG]] where he worked on [[thermodynamics]] and [[Chemical kinetics|reaction kinetics]]. Dieter Langbein's scientific career was characterized by working closely with experimental physicists as well as with chemists and biologists. He achieved this by joining Battelle-Institut e.V., Frankfurt am Main in 1964. His work on the splitting of the [[electronic band structure]] in magnetic fields together with E. Gerlach <ref>E. Gerlach and D. Langbein, Phys. Rev. 145, 449 - 457 (1966)</ref> led to a guest professorship at James Frank Institute, [[University of Chicago]], Illinois in 1967/1968 followed by a stay at the [[Battelle Memorial Institute]] in [[Columbus, Ohio]].  His research led to the later [[Hofstadter's butterfly]] of the electron's energy bands structure. In 1969 he receives the [[venia legendi]] for physics at Frankfurt University and in 1972 he becomes Honorary Professor.

Back at Battelle-Institute Frankfurt he turned to the field of [[Van der Waals force]]. After a Visiting Fellowship at the [[University of Canberra]], Australia he published in 1974 his book ''Theory of Van der Waals attraction''.

Around 1976 he learned about the fascination of research under [[microgravity]] conditions. He set up a table of about a dozen effects contributing to the separation of monotectic alloys during solidification observed in rocket experiments. His microgravity experiments with transparent liquids proved the importance of the [[Marangoni effect]]. He became a member of the managing committee of [[ELGRA]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.elgra.org/History.htm |title=How ELGRA was founded |publisher=www.elgra.org |accessdate=2008-11-09 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080511160427/http://www.elgra.org/History.htm |archivedate=2008-05-11 }}</ref> (European Low Gravity Research Association) in 1978, chairman of the German consulting group on fluid physics under low gravity and was scientific consultant at [[European Space Agency|ESA]], [[NASA]] and [[Japan Microgravity Centre|JAMIC]]. Together with the [[Kennedy Space Center]], Florida, he 1985 established The Microgravity Research Experiments (MICREX) Database, for which he was the principal investigator.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://exploration.grc.nasa.gov/fcarchive/media/micrex/exps/lang-d1a.html |title=Mixing and Demixing of Transparent Liquids (Run A and B) |publisher=MICREX database |accessdate=2008-11-09 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110525145139/http://exploration.grc.nasa.gov/fcarchive/media/micrex/exps/lang-d1a.html |archivedate=2011-05-25 }}</ref> The collaboration with NASA facilitated some more results, such as those related to the German Spacelab Mission <ref>Langbein, D.: Fluid Physics. In Proceedings of the Norderney Symposium on Scientific Results of the German Spacelab Mission D1, Norderney, Germany, August 27–29, 1986. (specifically pp. 101-102; post-flight)</ref> where he became friend with German physicist and astronaut [[Ulf Merbold]] and the advances in space research<ref>Langbein, D. "Motion of ensembles of spherical particles in a fluid due to g-jitter." Advances in Space Research 11:189-196 (1991).</ref> and other fluid physics studies.<ref>D. Langbein, J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 2 Supplement (1990) SA491-SA498</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://gltrs.grc.nasa.gov/reports/1998/TM-1998-207916.pdf |title=Dynamics of Liquids in Edges and Corners |publisher=NASA |accessdate=2008-11-09 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20061010143337/http://gltrs.grc.nasa.gov/reports/1998/TM-1998-207916.pdf |archivedate=2006-10-10 }}</ref>

In 1993 he left Battelle and continued his work at the Center of Applied Space Technology and Microgravity (ZARM) at the [[University of Bremen]], Germany.

== Publications ==
In 1969 Langbein published an article <ref>Dieter Langbein, Phys. Rev. 180, 633 - 648 The tight-binding and the Nearly-Free-Electron Approach to Lattice Electrons In external Magnetic Fields (1969)</ref> in which he demonstrated that the electron's energy sub-band disposal presents regularities which are connected to the [[Landau levels]].

In 1974 he published his first book, ''Theory of Van der Waals attraction''.<ref>Langbein, Dieter ''Theory of Van der Waals Attraction'', ( Springer-Verlag New York Heidelberg 1974)</ref>

In 2002 he published his second book ''Capillary Surfaces: Shape - Stability - Dynamics in particular under weightlessness'' about the [[capillary effect]].<ref>Langbein, Dieter; ''Capillary Surfaces: Shape - Stability - Dynamics in particular under weightlessness'', (Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg 2002)</ref>

Between 1956 and 2001 he published more than 160 articles.<ref>D. Langbein, Phys. Rev. B 2, 3371 - 3383 (1970)</ref><ref>D. Langbein, J. Phys. A: Gen. Phys. 4 No 4 (1971) 471-476</ref><ref>D. Langbein, J. Phys. A: Math. Nucl. Gen. 6 No 8 (1973) 1149-1168</ref><ref>D. Langbein, J. Phys. A: Math. Nucl. Gen. 7 No 9 (1974) 1117-1128</ref><ref>D. Langbein, J. Phys. A: Math. Gen. 8 No 10 (1975) 1593-1613</ref><ref>D. Langbein, J. Phys. A: Math. Gen. 9 No 4 (1976) 627-644</ref><ref>D. Langbein, J. Phys. A: Math. Gen. 10 No 6 (1977) 1031-1041</ref>
